Apply variable and value labels to a variable

Source: R/recode.R
jrelabel.Rd

jrelabel() attaches a variable label and/or value labels to any variable in a data frame. It is designed as a simple label applicator — it does not recode values, convert types, or compare variables. Use it to add labels after a recode, to fix missing labels, or to label any variable that needs them.

It has two forms. The one-variable form, jrelabel(MyData, Q1, labels = ...), returns the labeled variable for you to assign to a column, or with modify = TRUE labels the variable in the data frame directly. The list form, jrelabel(MyData, c(Q1, Q2, Q3), labels = ..., modify = TRUE), gives several variables the same value labels in one call – the way a set of survey items sharing one response scale is labeled – and always changes the data frame itself, so it takes modify = TRUE.

A variable label (var.label) can be attached to a variable of any type — the variable is returned unchanged apart from the new label, so dates stay dates, factors stay factors, and text stays text. Value labels (labels) can be applied to haven-labelled, plain numeric, and logical variables; logical values are stored as 1 (TRUE) and 0 (FALSE). Factor, character, and date/time variables cannot carry value labels, and jrelabel() refuses the labels argument for these; for factor and text variables the message names jencode as the fix.

jrelabel() never rebuilds the variable it is given. Existing value labels, SPSS-style missing values (na_values / na_range), Stata-style missing values, and the variable's class all pass through untouched unless an argument you supply replaces them: new value labels replace the existing ones (as VALUE LABELS does in SPSS), except that a declared missing value keeps its label unless the new set names it, as jrecode()'s labels argument keeps them, and a note names the labels kept; a new variable label replaces the old one. To change a declared value's label, name it in the new set, e.g. labels = "1=Low; 2=High; -99=No answer". On a column with Stata-style or SAS-style missing values, a marker that no case carries is declared only by its label, and it stays declared; name it by its marker to relabel it, e.g. labels = "1=Low; .c=Refused".

Both the labels and var.label arguments are optional in the one-variable form. If neither is supplied, the function returns the variable unchanged.

Usage

jrelabel(
  data,
  var,
  labels = NULL,
  var.label = NULL,
  vars = NULL,
  modify = FALSE,
  ...
)

Arguments

data

A data frame containing the variable.

var

The variable to label (unquoted, e.g. StatusR; a quoted name is accepted), or a c() of two or more for the list form (see the section below).

labels

Optional. A quoted string specifying value labels using the format "code=Label Text" with rules separated by semicolons. Accepted on haven-labelled, plain numeric, and logical variables only. A label may be written in quotes, with either mark, right after its equals sign, and a semicolon inside the quotes is then part of the label: "1=Yes; 9=\"Refused; not asked\"". An unquoted label reads as it is written.

Examples:

  • "1=Yes; 0=No"

  • "1=Employed; 2=Unemployed; 3=Student; 4=Retired"

var.label

Optional. A quoted string to use as the variable label (the description shown by jdesc(), jfreq(), etc.). If omitted, any existing variable label is preserved. If the variable has no existing label, no variable label is set. One-variable form only.

vars

Optional. For the list form: the variables' names in quotes, a stored or computed list such as vars = items or vars = c("Q1", "Q2"). Names typed without quotes go after the data frame, in a c().

modify

Logical. TRUE labels the variable(s) in the data frame directly, so no assignment is needed; the data frame must be given by its name (or set with juse()). Optional in the one-variable form, which still returns the variable; required in the list form. Default FALSE.

...

Not used. An input jrelabel() does not take – a misspelled argument – stops with "unused input" and the name as typed, in place of R's own "unused argument".

Value

The one-variable form: the variable with the requested labels applied, returned invisibly (nothing prints at the console), with or without modify = TRUE. The variable keeps its class: haven-labelled input stays haven-labelled with any declared SPSS-style or Stata-style missing values intact; plain numeric and logical input becomes haven_labelled when value labels are applied; any other type is returned unchanged apart from the labels. Without modify = TRUE, assign the result to a column to keep it (at the standard and full output levels a note says so after each call). Two assignment forms do that job:

  • Preserving: MyData$VarNameL <- jrelabel(MyData, VarName, ...) adds a labeled copy and keeps the original as it was.

  • Overwrite (the usual choice here): MyData$VarName <- jrelabel(MyData, VarName, ...) labels the variable in place. Labels change how values are shown, not the values, so there is normally nothing to keep a copy of.

SPSS users will recognize the pair from RECODE ... INTO new. and bare RECODE; for labels, SPSS's VALUE LABELS and VARIABLE LABELS always label in place, the overwrite form – which modify = TRUE gives directly.

The list form: the changed data frame, invisibly.

The list form

A c() of two or more variables after the data frame – or a stored list of names in quotes, vars = items – applies the same value labels to each variable, in the data frame itself:


jrelabel(MyData, c(Q1, Q2, Q3),
         labels = "1=Never; 2=Sometimes; 3=Often", modify = TRUE)

The SPSS equivalent is VALUE LABELS Q1 Q2 Q3 1 'Never' 2 'Sometimes' 3 'Often'. The form takes modify = TRUE and stops without it, offering the call with it added: a call that changes several variables returns the whole data frame, and assigning that to one column (MyData$Q1 <- jrelabel(...)) would put the data frame inside the column. It also returns the changed data frame, so e <- jrelabel(d, c(Q1, Q2), ..., modify = TRUE) labels d and keeps a copy in e. Every variable is checked before any is changed, so a call that stops changes nothing. A variable label names one variable and is refused in this form; give each its own call. A list in vars = follows these rules whatever its length, so a script that builds its list of names behaves the same when the list holds one name; c(Q1) after the data frame is the one-variable form.

See also

jrecode for recoding values with optional labels in a single step.

jstats for the package overview, workflow conventions, and complete function listing.

Examples

# Add value labels after a recode
df <- data.frame(Status = c(1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2))
df$StatusR <- ifelse(df$Status == 1, 1, 0)
df$StatusR <- jrelabel(df, StatusR, labels = "1=Yes; 0=No",
                       var.label = "Status (recoded)")
#> Note: This call changes df only if you assign the result:
#>   df$StatusR <- jrelabel(...)
#> 
#> To label StatusR in df directly, rerun with modify = TRUE:
#>   jrelabel(..., modify = TRUE)

# The same, labeling the variable in the data frame directly
jrelabel(df, StatusR, labels = "1=Yes; 0=No", modify = TRUE)
#> Value labels applied to StatusR in df.

# The data frame may also be given by name
df$StatusR <- jrelabel(data = df, StatusR, labels = "1=Yes; 0=No")
#> Note: This call changes df only if you assign the result:
#>   df$StatusR <- jrelabel(...)
#> 
#> To label StatusR in df directly, rerun with modify = TRUE:
#>   jrelabel(..., modify = TRUE)

# Add just a variable label
df$StatusR <- jrelabel(df, StatusR, var.label = "Employment Status")
#> Note: This call changes df only if you assign the result:
#>   df$StatusR <- jrelabel(...)
#> 
#> To label StatusR in df directly, rerun with modify = TRUE:
#>   jrelabel(..., modify = TRUE)

# Add just value labels
df$StatusR <- jrelabel(df, StatusR, labels = "1=Yes; 0=No")
#> Note: This call changes df only if you assign the result:
#>   df$StatusR <- jrelabel(...)
#> 
#> To label StatusR in df directly, rerun with modify = TRUE:
#>   jrelabel(..., modify = TRUE)

# Label a date variable (the variable stays a Date)
df$Enrolled <- as.Date(c("2024-01-15", "2024-02-01", "2024-01-20",
                         "2024-03-05", "2024-02-14", "2024-01-30"))
df$Enrolled <- jrelabel(df, Enrolled, var.label = "Enrollment date")
#> Note: This call changes df only if you assign the result:
#>   df$Enrolled <- jrelabel(...)
#> 
#> To label Enrolled in df directly, rerun with modify = TRUE:
#>   jrelabel(..., modify = TRUE)

# Several items that share one response scale: the list form
sv <- data.frame(Q1 = c(1, 3, 2), Q2 = c(2, 2, 3), Q3 = c(3, 1, 1))
jrelabel(sv, c(Q1, Q2, Q3), labels = "1=Never; 2=Sometimes; 3=Often",
         modify = TRUE)
#> Value labels applied to Q1, Q2, and Q3 in sv.

# The same from a stored list of names
items <- c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3")
jrelabel(sv, vars = items, labels = "1=Never; 2=Sometimes; 3=Often",
         modify = TRUE)
#> Value labels applied to Q1, Q2, and Q3 in sv.

# Using juse() default
juse(df)
#> Default data frame set to: df
df$StatusR <- jrelabel(StatusR, labels = "1=Active; 0=Inactive")
#> Note: This call changes df only if you assign the result:
#>   df$StatusR <- jrelabel(...)
#> 
#> To label StatusR in df directly, rerun with modify = TRUE:
#>   jrelabel(..., modify = TRUE)
juse(NULL)
#> Default data frame cleared.
